title: God Moves Into the Temple
overview: Solomon brings the sacred chest called the ark into the newly finished temple, a cloud of God's presence fills it, and he prays that God will hear everyone who turns toward this place.

parts.label: The ark comes home (vv. 1-11)
parts.note: At the big autumn festival, priests carry the ark, the chest holding the stone tablets of God's agreement with Israel, into the temple's innermost room beneath carved winged figures. A cloud then fills the building, the same sign of God's presence Israel knew in the desert, and it is so overwhelming the priests cannot stay inside.

parts.label: Solomon explains the cloud (vv. 12-21)
parts.note: Solomon tells everyone the dark cloud is not a threat but a sign that God has accepted this house as his home. He praises God for keeping his promise to David that David's son would be the one to build it.

parts.label: God too big for a building (vv. 22-30)
parts.note: Kneeling with raised hands, Solomon admits that even the highest heaven cannot hold God, so a temple certainly cannot, yet he speaks of God's 'Name' being there. Readers have long debated exactly what that phrase means for how God is present, but his request is clear: when people pray toward this place, hear from heaven and forgive.

parts.label: Seven kinds of trouble (vv. 31-53)
parts.note: Solomon lists hard situations: a disputed oath between neighbors, defeat in war, drought, famine and disease, a foreigner coming to pray, soldiers in battle, and the whole people carried off as captives. Many scholars think the strong focus on exile reflects the later time when Israel actually lived as captives in Babylon and this book was being completed.

parts.label: A blessing on the people (vv. 54-61)
parts.note: Solomon stands and blesses the crowd, saying none of God's good promises given through Moses has failed. He asks God to stay with them and turn their hearts toward him, so every nation would know the LORD is God.

parts.label: Two weeks of feasting (vv. 62-66)
parts.note: The offerings are so many that the middle of the courtyard has to serve as an extra altar. Most were fellowship offerings, where worshipers ate much of the meat, so this became a two week national feast before people from the far north to the far south went home glad.

think: Solomon says no building could ever hold God, yet he still hopes for one place where every cry gets heard; why do you think people so often want a particular place to bring their hopes and troubles?
